claim_checks.sentence: Wrong-level spine surgery persists because intraoperative fluoroscopy shows a few vertebrae at a time and the surgeon counts from whatever landmark is visible \citep{mayer2008,hsiang2011}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: The current method to prevent wrong-level spine surgery performed is by intra-operative X-ray which allows the surgeon to count the spine level one by one. Unfortunately, regardless of the above effort, wrong level spine surgery, albeit very uncommon, still happened.
claim_checks.fix: Hsiang supports two points: wrong-level surgery still happens, and the level is found by counting one by one on intraoperative X-ray. He never says the field shows only a few vertebrae or that the count starts from whatever landmark is visible. Get that from mayer2008 if it says so, or from another source. Alternatively reword the Hsiang part: 'Wrong-level spine surgery still occurs even though the level is confirmed by counting vertebrae one by one on intraoperative X-ray \citep{hsiang2011}.'

claim_checks.sentence: The field holds three or four bodies, so a count from the sacrum to a mid-thoracic level passes through several exposures each of which can be joined to the last one body off; a lumbosacral or thoracolumbar transitional vertebra shifts the count by one for the whole column; ribs are hard to number where a twelfth rib is absent or hypoplastic; and habitus, osteopenia and the scapular shadow degrade the mid-thoracic image most \citep{strong2021,hsiang2011}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: Congenital abnormal variant of spine anatomy in some patients such as four or six lumbar spines,[3] lumbarized sacrum, or congenital fusion of spinous processes. Very abnormal spine anatomy or deformity such as scoliosis and osteoporosis making it difficult to count the correct level. Adequate intra-operative X-rays are not possible in morbidly obese patients. ... This is especially common in the thoracic spine. ... The second case is more difficult because the lesion is located at the T3 and T4 level. Intraoperative x-ray localization at these levels is very difficult because the patient's shoulders obstruct the view.
claim_checks.fix: Hsiang supports these parts: lumbosacral variants (four or six lumbar vertebrae, lumbarized sacrum), osteoporosis, morbid obesity, and the thoracic spine being hardest. He does not mention a 3-4 body field, chaining exposures, thoracolumbar transitional vertebrae, or twelfth-rib anomalies, so those need strong2021 or another source. The shoulder obstruction he describes is at T3-T4, which is upper thoracic, not mid-thoracic. Suggested wording for the last clause: 'and obesity, osteoporosis and, in the upper thoracic spine, the shoulders degrade the image \citep{hsiang2011}'. Keep 'mid-thoracic' and 'scapular shadow' only if strong2021 says them.

claim_checks.sentence: With navigation, a tracked instrument is registered to a preoperative or intraoperative 3-D scan and the level is read off the registration; without it, the surgeon counts bodies on fluoroscopy that shows three or four at a time, up from the sacrum or down from a cervical landmark, across successive C-arm shots \citep{manbachi2018,hsiang2011,strong2021,mayer2008}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: The current method to prevent wrong-level spine surgery performed is by intra-operative X-ray which allows the surgeon to count the spine level one by one. ... Even though computer-assisted image guidance can help to reduce the risk of wrong level surgery,[6] this technology is not readily available in all hospitals
claim_checks.fix: The sentence cites Hsiang for two things he supports: counting one by one on intraoperative X-ray, and computer-assisted image guidance as the alternative. He says nothing about registration mechanics, three or four bodies per field, or counting up from the sacrum or down from a cervical landmark across shots. Those parts must come from manbachi2018, strong2021 or mayer2008. Hsiang can stay in the citation list, but none of those details should rest on him.

claim_checks.sentence: Navigation is not available in every hospital and not practical for every operation \citep{hsiang2011}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: Even though computer-assisted image guidance can help to reduce the risk of wrong level surgery,[6] this technology is not readily available in all hospitals, and it is not practical to apply to all spine surgeries.

claim_checks.evidence_quote: "We fill the gap by providing an open-access Cervical Spine X-ray Atlas (CSXA), which includes 4963 raw PNG images and 4963 annotated images with JSON format" ... "Cervical curvature: C2-7 Cobb angle is measured from the inferior endplate of C2 to the inferior endplate of C7, C2-6 Cobb is measured from the inferior endplate of C2 to the inferior endplate of C6, and C2-7 SVA is centroid of C2 and the posterior superior aspect of C7" ... claim_checks.fix: No change needed. The article supports 'annotated' (surgeon keypoints) and 'real' (hospital patients) directly. The project's own inventory also records CSXA as 4,963 lateral cervical films.

claim_checks.evidence_quote: arXiv preprint, Related Work: "Wang et al. proposed a parallax-free X-ray image stitching methodology by restricting the X-ray camera to only undergo pure rotation [33, 34]. To compensate for translation between the C-arm camera and the scene, the patient bed was translated with the same translational parameters as the X-ray source. The movement of patient bed in the surgery room is not practical in most surgical environments. Instead, this solution can be delivered by a robotic C-arm platform that uses kinematics to enforce the rotational motion."
claim_checks.fix: The substance holds: the source translation is cancelled by moving the bed, or by a robotic C-arm, so the acquisition is a pure rotation. But Fotouhi et al. only report this remedy; it belongs to Wang et al. (Med Image Anal 2010;14(5):674-686, and MICCAI 2009), cited as [33, 34], and the paper never says 'tracked table'. Suggested wording: '...cancelling the source translation by moving the patient bed with it (or with a robotic C-arm) so the acquisition becomes a pure rotation \citep{wang2010parallax,fotouhi2021}...'. Add Wang et al. 2010 as the primary citation for this half of the sentence.

claim_checks.sentence: A radiograph integrates all depths, so under a translating cone-beam source no single two-dimensional mapping aligns every structure in two frames; parallax is a geometric constraint and not an engineering nuisance, and the published remedies---cancelling the translation with a tracked table, or reconstructing an orthographic mosaic---need hardware a freehand sweep does not have \citep{fotouhi2021}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: arXiv preprint, Proposed Solution: "Our mapping for stitching is no longer a homography; instead, it directly uses the projection matrices." Methods: "µ(d, i, m, n) is the ray characterized by the projection matrix Pi and pixel coordinates (xm, yn) in the i-th image". Data: "We generated the training data by simulating realistic digitally-reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) using the physics-based DeepDRR pipeline". Against the claim, the Conclusion says: "our solution naturally allows for both translation and rotations of the X-ray camera and does not impose any constraints regarding the motion." TMI abstract: "Our work provides evidence that reconstruction of orthographic mosaics is possible with realistic motions of the C-arm involving both translation and rotation."
claim_checks.fix: The paper does not say it needs special hardware. It says it imposes no constraint on C-arm motion. What it does need is a known projection matrix (a calibrated pose) for every frame, and its experiments used simulated DeepDRR images whose poses were known. A freehand sweep does not supply those poses without tracking or calibration. Suggested wording: '...or reconstructing an orthographic mosaic, which needs a known projection matrix for every frame---require either motorised hardware or per-frame pose, neither of which a freehand sweep has \citep{wang2010parallax,fotouhi2021}.'

claim_disagreements: Claim 'The orthographic-mosaic remedy (Fotouhi et al.) needs hardware a freehand sweep does not have': the resolver says partly_supported; I would say not_supported, because the source leans the other way. The source never names any hardware. It says the method needs a projection matrix for every frame, and it frames itself as removing motion constraints. arXiv 2003.02959, Proposed Solution: "provides stitching of X-ray images with no constraints on the motion of the X-ray camera. Our mapping for stitching is no longer a homography; instead, it directly uses the projection matrices." Conclusion: "our solution naturally allows for both translation and rotations of the X-ray camera and does not impose any constraints regarding the motion." TMI abstract (PubMed/Europe PMC): "reconstruction of orthographic mosaics is possible with realistic motions of the C-arm involving both translation and rotation." The projection matrices come from simulation: "We generated the training data by simulating realistic digitally-reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) using the physics-based DeepDRR pipeline". The paper never says how a real C-arm would supply them. That tracking or calibration is needed is the citing author's inference. A supportable version would be: 'needs a known projection matrix for every frame, which a freehand sweep does not provide'.

Claim 'cancelling the translation with a tracked table': I agree with partly_supported, but the reason should be stated. The source never says 'tracked', and the remedy belongs to Wang et al. [33,34], not to Fotouhi et al. arXiv Related Work: "Wang et al. proposed a parallax-free X-ray image stitching methodology by restricting the X-ray camera to only undergo pure rotation [33, 34]. To compensate for translation between the C-arm camera and the scene, the patient bed was translated with the same translational parameters as the X-ray source. The movement of patient bed in the surgery room is not practical in most surgical environments. Instead, this solution can be delivered by a robotic C-arm platform". Citing fotouhi2021 for this is a secondary citation. Cite Wang, Traub, Weidert, Heining, Euler and Navab (Parallax-free intra-operative X-ray image stitching) directly, or say 'reviewed in'.

claim_checks.sentence: One quaternary centre placed 179 preoperative gold fiducials over 38 months, 176 of them thoracic, at a mean of 51.9 minutes and 183\,mGy each, purely to mark a level \citep{siminski2023}: at a median inpatient \$33.78 and a mean \$37.45 per operating-room minute in FY2014 dollars before physician fees, roughly 30--40\,\% more today \citep{childers2018}, \$1{,}750--\$1{,}950 per patient, a proxy since the marker is placed in a fluoroscopy or CT suite rather than a theatre.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "No wrong-level surgery occurred in these 179 consecutive cases, of which 176 were at the thoracic levels."; "Mean procedure duration (range) (min) a 51.9 (20–114)"; "The mean radiation dose was 183.43 mGy (range, 13–805 mGy)"; "Preoperative fiducial marker placement performed in a dedicated imaging suite"; "Fluoroscopy was used to place the gold fiducial marker in 143 patients (80%), with CT used in 36 (20%)."
claim_checks.fix: The Siminski numbers and the imaging-suite setting are supported. 'Quaternary' is not: replace it with 'One centre (Mayo Clinic, Rochester)' or 'one single-institution series'. The arithmetic is consistent: 51.9 × $33.78 = $1,753 and 51.9 × $37.45 = $1,944. The per-minute costs and the 30–40% inflation factor must be checked against childers2018 separately. Siminski puts the marker itself at about US $50 ('costing approximately US $50 at our institution'), which the proxy leaves out.

claim_checks.sentence: Against the alternative that is priced, a thoracic gold fiducial costs 51.9 minutes and 183\,mGy in a separate visit \citep{siminski2023} while a thoracic sweep costs the three to five intraoperative minutes above---two quantities that are not commensurable, one being a scheduled procedure on another day, so the comparison is offered as an order of magnitude.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "Mean procedure duration (range) (min) a 51.9 (20–114)"; "The mean radiation dose was 183.43 mGy (range, 13–805 mGy)"; "Gold fiducial marker placement typically occurs on an outpatient basis the day before surgery, though on occasion, it is done the morning of the operation."; "Mean No. of days when operation was performed after placement (range) 3.6 days (0–92)"
claim_checks.fix: Supported, with two nuances that could be stated. First, 51.9 min and 183 mGy are means over the whole cohort of 179, which includes one C7, one L3 and one L4 case, not thoracic-only means. Second, placement is usually the day before surgery but sometimes the morning of the operation (range 0–92 days). A more careful version: 'in a separate procedure, usually the day before surgery'.

claim_checks.sentence: The cost of avoiding the count is visible at one quaternary centre, which placed preoperative percutaneous gold fiducial markers in 179 patients over 38 months, 176 of them thoracic, at a mean of 51.9 minutes and 183\,mGy each, solely to mark a level for the surgeon \citep{siminski2023}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "A total of 179 patients (104 female) underwent gold fiducial marker placement."; "between January 3, 2019, and March 16, 2022"; "No wrong-level surgery occurred in these 179 consecutive cases, of which 176 were at the thoracic levels."; "Mean procedure duration (range) (min) a 51.9 (20–114)"; "The mean radiation dose was 183.43 mGy (range, 13–805 mGy)"; "The primary benefit of gold fiducial marker placement is to allow the surgeon to quickly and safely localize the correct vertebral level"
claim_checks.fix: All numbers are supported. Replace 'one quaternary centre' with 'one centre (Mayo Clinic, Rochester)' or 'one single-institution series', since the paper does not describe itself as quaternary.

claim_checks.sentence: A lumbar walk of two exposures is therefore about a minute and a mid-thoracic walk of three to four about two to three, against roughly fifteen minutes reported for fluoroscopic level counting in thoracic surgery \citep{mongardi2021,upadhyaya2012} and a preoperative CT-guided fiducial that buys three minutes in theatre for fourteen in the CT suite and a second visit \citep{keil2024,siminski2023}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "the average procedural time was similar (51.19 minutes for CT and 52.09 minutes for FL)"; "Average procedural time (range) (min) 51.19 (31–114)" [CT column, Table 2]; "Additionally, although not directly assessed in our review, fiducial marker placement has been shown to greatly reduce intraoperative FL time and ultimately operative time."; "Gold fiducial marker placement typically occurs on an outpatient basis the day before surgery, though on occasion, it is done the morning of the operation."
claim_checks.fix: Siminski supports only the second visit. It did not measure intraoperative time saved ('not directly assessed in our review'). Its CT-guided room time is 51.19 min (31–114), physician entry to room exit, not fourteen minutes. Credit the 3 and 14 minute figures to keil2024 alone, and verify them there, since they were not checked here. For example: '...a preoperative CT-guided fiducial that buys three minutes in theatre for fourteen in the CT suite \citep{keil2024}, and in a larger series about 51 minutes of room time in a separate visit, usually the day before surgery \citep{siminski2023}.'

claim_disagreements: Claim 3 ('A thoracic gold fiducial takes a mean 51.9 min and 183 mGy, done in a separate, scheduled visit on another day'): the resolver says supported. I say partly_supported. The paper says placement 'typically occurs on an outpatient basis the day before surgery, though on occasion, it is done the morning of the operation', and Table 1 gives 'Mean No. of days when operation was performed after placement (range) 3.6 days (0–92)'. Some placements were on the day of surgery, so 'on another day' is typical, not universal. Also, 51.9 min ('Mean procedure duration (range) (min) 51.9 (20–114)', timed from room entry to room exit) and 183.43 mGy are means over all 179 cases, including the C7, L3 and L4 placements. They are not thoracic-only figures.

Claim 5 (keil2024 and siminski2023 cited together for 'buys three minutes in theatre for fourteen in the CT suite and a second visit'): the resolver says partly_supported. For siminski2023 I say not_supported, apart from the second visit. Siminski gives CT-guided suite time as 'Average procedural time (range) (min) 51.19 (31–114)' (Table 2; the text says '51.19 minutes for CT and 52.09 minutes for FL'), which does not match fourteen. On theatre time it says 'although not directly assessed in our review, fiducial marker placement has been shown to greatly reduce intraoperative FL time and ultimately operative time'. So nothing in Siminski supports 'three minutes in theatre', and its CT-suite figure is about 3.6 times the one in the sentence. Only the separate visit is supported ('typically ... the day before surgery'). The numbers have to come from keil2024 alone. The sentence should either credit them to keil2024 alone or drop siminski2023 from that clause.

claim_checks.sentence: In theatre the standard technique is unchanged: needles are placed every few levels and counted cephalad from the sacrum on lateral fluoroscopy, or ribs are counted on an anteroposterior film, and surgeons disagree even on which structure to count, the pedicle for 67 % and the spinous process for 49 % of respondents [strong2021, mayer2008].
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "Classically, a series of needles are placed every few levels counting from the sacrum in a cephalad fashion. This is most frequently performed with lateral fluoroscopic views." ... "anteroposterior (AP) projection on fluoroscopy is the most effective way of visualizing the thoracic spine. However, AP projections can be very technique-dependent and require extensive knowledge of anatomy and experience using fluoroscopy to count spinal levels." ... "there is variability as to which anatomical landmark to use for localization, either pedicle (67% in thoracic and 59% in lumbar) or the spinous process (49% in thoracic and 52% in lumbar). 1, 2"
claim_checks.fix: The needle technique is quoted almost word for word. Two problems. (1) 67% and 49% are the THORACIC figures; the lumbar ones are 59% and 52%, and the primary survey (Mayer 2014, Spine J, key mayer2008) calls the landmark 'the facet joint with corresponding pedicle'. Suggested wording: '...the facet joint and pedicle for 67% and the spinous process for 49% of respondents in the thoracic spine (59% and 52% in the lumbar; more than one answer allowed)'. (2) Strong calls needle counting 'traditional' and 'classical' but never says the technique is 'unchanged'. Soften to 'the traditional technique'. Strong supports AP fluoroscopy as the usual thoracic view for counting levels, but does not describe counting ribs on an AP film as the alternative standard.

claim_checks.sentence: The field holds three or four bodies, so a count from the sacrum to a mid-thoracic level passes through several exposures each of which can be joined to the last one body off; a lumbosacral or thoracolumbar transitional vertebra shifts the count by one for the whole column; ribs are hard to number where a twelfth rib is absent or hypoplastic; and habitus, osteopenia and the scapular shadow degrade the mid-thoracic image most [strong2021, hsiang2011].
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "Several factors, especially in the thoracic spine, make accurate localization difficult, including morbid obesity, previous spine surgery, infections, osteoporosis, anatomical variations including transitional vertebrae, scapular shadowing (in the upper- to midthoracic levels), variation in the number of rib-bearing vertebrae, hemivertebrae, and fused vertebrae." ... "Correct localization is usually most problematic in the midthoracic spine where the pathology is difficult to localize radiographically." ... "Counting up from the lumbosacral junction can also be particularly difficult in cases of transitional lumbosacral anatomy." ... "transitional anatomy or additional or fewer ribs can significantly compromise accuracy, especially with needle or external marker localization." Fig. 3 legend: "Intraoperative fluoroscopic images were stitched together with the needle pointing at the level of the T10 pedicle."
claim_checks.fix: Strong supports the confounders: habitus/obesity, osteoporosis, scapular shadowing, transitional vertebrae, fewer or additional ribs, and the midthoracic spine being hardest. Strong does not support 'the field holds three or four bodies' or the idea that successive exposures are joined one body off. Neither appears in Strong or in the co-cited Hsiang 2011 (PMC3108446, searched). Either cite a source that states the field size or drop the number, e.g. 'a count from the sacrum to a mid-thoracic level spans several stitched exposures'. Also replace 'a twelfth rib absent or hypoplastic' with Strong's 'additional or fewer ribs', and say 'osteoporosis' (Strong's word) rather than 'osteopenia'.

claim_checks.sentence: With navigation, a tracked instrument is registered to a preoperative or intraoperative 3-D scan and the level is read off the registration; without it, the surgeon counts bodies on fluoroscopy that shows three or four at a time, up from the sacrum or down from a cervical landmark, across successive C-arm shots [manbachi2018, hsiang2011, strong2021, mayer2008].
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "The use of intraoperative navigation in spinal surgery has increased immensely since the mid-2000s with the development of intraoperative cone-beam CT and 3D fluoroscopic guidance. Irrespective of the type of intraoperative image acquisition used, spinal navigation can be used to augment any approach, including intraoperative surgical spine-level validation." ... "Classically, a series of needles are placed every few levels counting from the sacrum in a cephalad fashion." ... "After counting down from C2, the disc space of interest is noted" (preoperative PMMA marking under biplanar fluoroscopy) ... "Any discrepancies between cranial-caudal counting or caudal-cranial counting due to anatomical variation will be resolved by reviewing preoperative imaging"
claim_checks.fix: Strong supports: navigation for level validation, counting cephalad from the sacrum, cranial-to-caudal counting from C2 (described for the preoperative marking procedures), and stitched successive images (Fig. 3). Strong gives no field size ('three or four at a time'), and Hsiang 2011 does not either. Remove the number, or add a citation that states it.

claim_checks.sentence: Needles are placed every few levels and counted cephalad from the sacrum on lateral fluoroscopy, and surgeons disagree on what to count: in a national survey permitting multiple answers, the pedicle for 67 % of respondents in the thoracic spine and 59 % in the lumbar, the spinous process for 49 % and 52 %, the number of respondents not stated in the sources assembled here [strong2021, mayer2008].
claim_checks.evidence_quote: Strong 2021: "Classically, a series of needles are placed every few levels counting from the sacrum in a cephalad fashion. This is most frequently performed with lateral fluoroscopic views." ... "either pedicle (67% in thoracic and 59% in lumbar) or the spinous process (49% in thoracic and 52% in lumbar)." Mayer 2014 (co-cited as mayer2008), PubMed 24012429 abstract: "A total of 2,338 surgeons received the survey, 532 opened the survey, and 173 completed it (7.4% response rate)." ... "Some questions asked surgeons to select as many responses as applicable" ... "The facet joint with corresponding pedicle was the most commonly used anatomic landmark for localization of thoracic and lumbar surgeries (67% and 59%, respectively), followed by the spinous process (49% and 52%, respectively)."
claim_checks.fix: The four percentages and the needle technique match Strong exactly, and 'multiple answers' is confirmed by Mayer. The closing clause is wrong: the co-cited survey states its sample. The landmark should read 'the facet joint with corresponding pedicle'.

claim_checks.sentence: The level is identified intraoperatively on fluoroscopy that shows three or four bodies in a 9-inch field, by placing a needle and counting cephalad from the sacrum, or by counting ribs on an anteroposterior film [strong2021, mayer2008].
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "Classically, a series of needles are placed every few levels counting from the sacrum in a cephalad fashion. claim_checks.sentence: It is not removable by checklists: chart review of insured wrong-site cases found the Universal Protocol would have prevented 62\,\% of them under ideal conditions \citep{kwaan2006}, and wrong-site events continued at a steady rate in the protocol era \citep{stahel2010}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: Among 2,826,367 operations at insured institutions during the study period, 25 nonspine wrong-site operations were identified ... Medical records were available for review in 13 cases. ... Under optimal conditions, the Joint Commission on Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations Universal Protocol might have prevented 8 (62%) of 13 cases.
claim_checks.fix: The 62% figure is correct, but three things need fixing. (1) The paper says 'might have prevented', not 'would have'. (2) 62% is 8 of the 13 cases with reviewable records, not of all 25 insured cases. (3) The series is explicitly NONSPINE, so it cannot speak to wrong-level spine surgery, which is what 'It' refers to here. Suggested wording: 'chart review of 13 insured nonspine wrong-site cases judged that the Universal Protocol, under optimal conditions, might have prevented eight (62\,\%) \citep{kwaan2006}'. If the spine point is kept, say plainly that the evidence comes from nonspine cases.

claim_checks.sentence: Chart review of 13 insured wrong-site cases judged eight preventable under ideal conditions \citep{kwaan2006}; a 2012 systematic review located a single study assessing prevention, in which site-verification protocols failed to prevent about one-third of cases \citep{longo2012}; and the recommended safeguard, imaging after exposure against a marked fixed structure \citep{devine2010}, is itself another count.

(b) Longo 2012's 'only one study assessed preventative strategies ... did not prevent about one-third of the cases' reads like Kwaan 2006's own conclusion ('could have prevented only two thirds of the examined cases'). If so, this sentence presents one study as two independent findings. Check Longo's reference list before keeping both clauses as separate evidence.

claim_checks.sentence: \section*{What the protocol era shows} Kwaan and colleagues reviewed insured wrong-site cases and judged that the Universal Protocol, applied under ideal conditions, would have prevented 62\,\% of them \citep{kwaan2006}.

RESULTS: ... 25 nonspine wrong-site operations were identified ... Medical records were available for review in 13 cases. ... claim_checks.evidence_quote: "Positioning the C-arm to a given target view required an average of 36.4±33.2 s using FluoroSim, compared with 41.0±30.9 s for conventional fluoro-hunting. "On average, fluoroscopic exposure time required to achieve a given target view decreased by 4.1 s with FluoroSim—specifically, 4.7 s of fluoro-hunting time versus 0.5 s for FluoroSim." The 49 s comes from Matthews 2007 (PMID 17986885, abstract: navigated 46 s, 95% CI 41-51; scout-based 49 s, 95% CI 44-53). Together they give the 36-49 s range. claim_checks.evidence_quote: "Conventional: Store all X-ray views required for repositioning, and final C-arm position using an external marker."  |  "However, when X-ray images are acquired to verify and adjust the C-arm pose, the conventional approach substantially outperforms the proposed system."  |  "With the conventional method, a total of 16 X-rays where required to restore 6 poses yielding, on average, 2.76 X-rays per C-arm position."

Also, Run 3 was dropped because the technician restored the wrong view, so the figure leaves out a gross error: "We have omitted Run 3 from the quantitative evaluation since the X-ray technician erroneously restored the caudal oblique view requested in the previous run."

claim_checks.sentence: The only published figure for how far a mobile C-arm lands from an intended pose is 16.7$\,\pm\,$6.3\,mm, measured against an optical tracker, and that is the residual \emph{after} the operator has iterated with fluoroscopy \citep{unberath2018}; at a 35\,mm lumbar pitch it is about half a vertebral body against a search window of 0.6.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: The same table gives a second figure: "Proposed ... mean distance ± SD 51.6 ± 19.2 mm". The setting is narrow: "we setup an experiment mimicking pelvic trauma surgery using an anthropomorphic Sawbones pelvis phantom"; "The experimental design described here is limited since only a single X-ray technician and four runs were considered." The experiment section never names the C-arm or calls it mobile; 'mobile C-arms' appears only in the Discussion. Related work reports angles only: Matthews 2007 (PMID 17986885) abstract: "Deviations from the original projection were minimal for both navigated (0.9 degrees ...) and non-navigated repositioning (0.8 degrees ...)"; De Silva 2018 (PMID 29487882, PMC5812884) reports conventional positioning error in degrees only.
claim_checks.fix: Replace the uniqueness claim with a bounded one, for example: 'The only translational figure we found for how far an unassisted C-arm lands when a technician restores a recorded pose is 16.7 +/- 6.3 mm (mean displacement of a gantry-mounted marker tracked optically; one technician, a draped pelvis phantom, pelvic inlet, outlet and oblique views), and that is the residual after the technician had refined the pose with fluoroscopy [unberath2018].' Drop 'mobile' or write 'a C-arm'. 'The only published figure' cannot be checked, and the cited paper itself also reports 51.6 mm for its AR-guided arm.

claim_checks.sentence: The only published figure for how far a mobile C-arm lands from an intended pose is 16.7$\,\pm\,$6.3\,mm, measured against an optical tracker, and that is the residual \emph{after} the operator has iterated with fluoroscopy \citep{unberath2018}; at a 35\,mm lumbar pitch it is about half a vertebral body against a search window of 0.6.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: The arithmetic holds (16.7/35 = 0.48). But the source measured 3-D Euclidean displacement of a marker on the gantry, not a cranio-caudal shift of the image: "We state residuals averaged over all C-arm poses separately for translation and rotation and compute the mean Euclidean displacement and angular deviation of the reference marker". The anatomy was a pelvis, not a lumbar spine. The paper's only image-space residual is in pixels and is never converted to mm: "Table 2 Projection domain keypoint displacement in pixels (px) Proposed Conventional on first try Conventional 210 ± 105 px 257 ± 171 px 68 ± 36 px".
claim_checks.fix: Make it conditional: 'if all of it fell along the cranio-caudal axis, at a 35 mm lumbar pitch it would be about half a vertebral body (0.48) against a search window of 0.6'. This matches the manuscript's next sentence, which says no axis-resolved figure exists.

claim_disagreements: Claim 3 ('This is the only published figure for how far a mobile C-arm lands from an intended pose'): resolver said partly_supported. I would call it not_supported. One source cannot back a claim that no other figure exists, and this paper contradicts it itself: Table 1 ('C-arm pose differences as per infrared marker tracking') gives a second figure for the same thing, 'Proposed ... 51.6 ± 19.2 mm'. The setting is also narrow: 'only a single X-ray technician and four runs were considered', on an 'anthropomorphic Sawbones pelvis phantom', and 'We have omitted Run 3 from the quantitative evaluation'. The paper does use the word 'mobile', but only in the Discussion and about the general class of device ('not yet widely available in mobile C-arms since these systems are usually non-robotic'). It never names the C-arm used in the experiment.

claim_checks.sentence: No published system detects and names vertebrae from the content of a real intraoperative fluoroscopic image at a recall high enough to support counting, and no per-vertebra recall on real fluoroscopy is published at all: the simulation-to-real literature reports landmark error in millimetres ... \citep{bier2019}, and the one method reporting 100\,\% vertebral localization in theatre transfers labels from the same patient's preoperative CT or MRI by registration rather than recognising anything in the radiograph \citep{levelcheck2016}.
claim_checks.evidence_quote: "The success rate was 100% at 26 seconds (200 multi-starts), 99.97% at 18 seconds (150 multi-starts), 99.86% at 13 seconds (100 multi-starts), and 99.3% at 7 seconds (50 multi-starts)." / "For spine level localization, the process requires only that the target vertebrae are labeled in the preoperative image - e.g., a single point click on the vertebral bodies of interest - and those same labels are in turn automatically localized on intraoperative fluoroscopy." / "Twenty consecutive patients undergoing thoracolumbar spine surgery, for whom both a preoperative CT scan and an intraoperative mobile radiograph were available, were retrospectively analyzed." / "Future work also includes using a pre-operative MRI as an alternative to CT"
claim_checks.fix: Supported: the 100% figure and the mechanism (labels placed on the preoperative image and transferred by registration). Not supported by this paper: 'or MRI'. Lo 2015 uses CT only and lists MRI as future work. Also, the 100% is a registration success rate (mPDE < 5 mm over 10,000 trials) that falls with computation budget. It was measured retrospectively on mobile radiographs of 20 patients, not run live in theatre and not on fluoroscopy. Suggested wording: '...and the one method reporting 100\,\% vertebral localization on intraoperative images (all 10,000 registration trials within 5\,mm on mobile radiographs of 20 patients, analysed retrospectively) transfers labels from the same patient's preoperative CT by registration rather than recognising anything in the radiograph \citep{levelcheck2016}'. To keep 'or MRI', cite the MR-LevelCheck extension as well: De Silva et al., Phys Med Biol 2017;62(2):684-701, doi 10.1088/1361-6560/62/2/684, PMID 28050972.
